title: The Ownership 100
standfirst: The definitive ranked ledger of who owns Africa's most valuable brands — the phone in your hand, the channel on your screen, the drink in your glass. Ranked by continental reach and value at stake; every entry links to its sourced file. The inaugural cohort maps the brands the desk has investigated; we are building it out to a full 100.
methodology: Each entry is drawn from a published Who's Buying Africa file or a deal in the ownership tracker, with the owner and headquarters sourced to named reporting. 'Retained' means African-owned; 'Exported' means the controlling equity now sits offshore; 'Contested' marks a brand where ownership is live — being sold, or being brought home. Ranking is by continental reach, value at stake and cultural centrality, assessed by the desk; it is a considered editorial ordering, not a market-cap table. Authorship is treated separately from ownership on purpose: many of the highest-ranked brands are African-authored and foreign-owned — that gap is the story the ledger exists to make legible.

entries.note: The best-selling phone brand across Africa — authored for the continent, wholly Chinese-owned.
The pipe that carries African football and Nollywood to the continent is now controlled from Paris.
Kenya's crown jewel: majority control sits with Vodacom, and above it Vodafone in London.
Big enough to be a takeover target, it stayed public, African and widely held. No one controls it.
Strategic heavy industry at continental scale, majority-owned by its African founder.
Nigeria authored the loyalty; Singapore, Jakarta and now the US own the company that banks it.
The grocery backbone of the continent, still South African-owned via public markets and the state pension fund.
Global scale across dozens of countries and never sold the cap table — value compounds for an African family.
The most concentrated African ownership on the desk: one Nigerian owns every share.
A marula liqueur that could only come from Southern Africa, now inside a Dutch brewer.
African-founded, still independent, and itself an acquirer of African companies.
Authored in Lagos, owned in San Francisco — and now buying other Nigerian fintechs onto a foreign rail.
Sold as the essence of Kenya, controlled from London for years, now heading for Tokyo.
A national institution controlled from Amsterdam — the same portfolio as Amarula.
The African acquirer the desk roots for: scaled across the continent by buying, not being bought.
One of Nigeria's most important financial rails, ultimately offshore-owned.
Often called the continent's e-commerce champion — German-incubated, foreign-founded, New-York-listed.
The culture is authored by Nigerians; the majority equity is owned by a US major. The founders kept the mic.

A world-beating brand that under-earns; the fix — outside capital — is forcing the ownership question in real time.
